newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korean won drops to all-time low.
newsitem.headline: South Korean won drops to all-time low.

text.p: The South Korean won dropped to a record low against the dollar on Monday, partly driven by speculation that the central bank was allowing the currency to decline to boost exports and cover a ballooning trade deficit.
Dealers said the Bank of Korea stepped into the market three times to ease the won's fall, but not convincingly enough to persuade them that it wanted to put the brakes on.
The won ended at 828.80 against the dollar, an all-time low, after opening at 824.20 and touching a low of 830.00. It has depreciated by seven percent from the end of last year.
"Some traders feel that the Bank of Korea is expressing the government's wish to see the won depreciate in order to push up exports," said a Western bank trader, who asked not to be named.

South Korea's trade deficit ballooned to $11.6 billion in the first seven months of the year against $6.5 billion a year earlier. Some economists predict the shortfall this year could reach $20 billion.
A central bank official denied stepping into the market. The bank has never acknowledged intervention.

"Today's situation was unusual, because normally the market follows the central bank's lead," said the managing director of a local merchant bank. "But today, the market basically ignored the central bank, because the bank was not aggressive in its dollar sales."
"I think players were actually trying to force the central bank into the market, to show them where the ceiling for the dollar is," he said.

However, other traders said the central bank did not aggressively intervene because it expects the dollar will fall next month on an inflow of new funds when the foreign ownership ceiling in the stock market is raised.
On October 1, the foreign limit will rise to 20 percent from the current 18 percent.
Traders said banks were eager to buy the dollar despite the interventions because of the need to meet scheduled import settlements and cover short positions.

South Korean exports have been shrinking due to weakening price competitiveness following the fall of the yen against the dollar and the plummeting price of major export items, such as semiconductors and steel.
But many fear that sharp falls in the won could also fuel inflation, as South Korea is heavily dependent on raw material imports.
"It's a sort of puzzle for the government," said the merchant bank managing director. "A lower won helps exports, but then the price of imports become more expensive."
Seoul was willing to take a chance on inflation in order to scale back the trade deficit, some analysts said.
"I believe the government view is that the effect of depreciating the won can be contained," said Yoo Tae-ho, managing director of the private Daewoo Economic Research Institute.
